definition: In this historical psychology usage, total recall refers to a form of association in which one mental item brings back another as a whole, rather than only in part or by a narrowed feature. James presents it as a proposed label for a type of recall closely overlapping what was commonly called association by similarity.

provenance.scope: Source record fca72454f1995c69b072; pinned source text

reasons: The packet supports that James proposed “total recall” as a better term and that it nearly matches “association by similarity,” but it does not explicitly support the added gloss that one mental item brings back another “as a whole” rather than “only in part” or by a “narrowed feature.”
The wording “in this historical psychology usage” is broader than the packet, which only shows James’s proposed nomenclature in a specific text passage, not a settled historical usage.

The packet does not explicitly define “total recall” as bringing back an associate “as a whole” rather than “in part” or by narrowed features. The passage only suggests alternative labels (“Total recall, partial recall, and focalized recall, of associates, would be better terms”) without stating the “whole vs part” meaning in those terms.

While the packet does support a connection between James’s wording and “association by similarity” (it discusses “association by similarity” and explains a choice of terminology), the specific claim that “total recall” is a proposed label for a recall type “closely overlapping” that process is not stated with enough precision to fully support the definition as written.
